title: Local potentials and smooth circle-bundle connection data

items.title: Finite-real supremum and infimum domain

references.title: Infimum and supremum (Wikipedia)
Least-upper-bound property (Wikipedia)
W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 1
John K. Hunter, An Introduction to Real Analysis
MIT 18.100A, Complete Lecture Notes

items.statement:
Use the real ordered field of [[def-real-numbers]] and [[def-complete-ordered-field]]. For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb R$ bounded above, $\sup S$ denotes the unique real upper bound $u$ such that $u\le v$ for every upper bound $v$. Existence is the least-upper-bound property established for these reals by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]; if $u,u'$ both satisfy it, $u\le u'$ and $u'\le u$ imply equality. The notation is restricted to this domain.

For nonempty $S$ bounded below, use [[def-infimum]] and [[thm-infimum-property]]: $\inf S=-\sup(-S)$, where $-S=\{-s:s\in S\}$. Indeed a lower bound $l$ for $S$ gives the upper bound $-l$ for $-S$; negating its least upper bound gives a lower bound for $S$ greater than every other one.

Neither $\sup\varnothing$ nor $\inf\varnothing$ is defined in $\mathbb R$: every real is an upper and lower bound, with no least upper or greatest lower bound. If another construction stipulates the value zero for an empty path family, that stipulation is a separate total definition, not $\sup\varnothing=0$. Infinite values require an explicitly specified extended ordered set; no extended-real field operations are introduced here.

items.title: Real metric and pseudometric convention

references.title: Metric space (Wikipedia)
Ultrametric space (Wikipedia)
W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 2
T. Tao, Analysis II, 3rd ed., Ch. 1
Pseudometric space (Wikipedia)
R. Gardner, Introduction to Topology, notes on Munkres Section 20: The Metric Topology (East Tennessee State University)

items.statement:
Let $X$ be a set and use the ordered real field of [[def-real-numbers]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and [[def-ordered-field]]. In the convention of [[def-metric-space]], a **real metric** is a function $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying, for all $x,y,z\in X$, separation $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$, symmetry $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ and the triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. A **real pseudometric** replaces separation by $d(x,x)=0$ and retains the other two axioms. All values are finite real numbers. Neither definition assumes nonnegativity as an additional axiom.

For either structure, put $B_d(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$ for real $r>0$. The induced topology consists of the subsets $O\subseteq X$ for which every $x\in O$ admits $r>0$ with $B_d(x,r)\subseteq O$. After the nonnegativity deduction in the well-definedness lemma, these balls form a basis: $x\in B_d(x,r)$ by reflexivity, and if $z\in B_d(x,r)\cap B_d(y,s)$, the positive radius $t=\min\{r-d(x,z),s-d(y,z)\}$ has $B_d(z,t)$ contained in that intersection by the triangle inequality. This argument also works for pseudometrics and for empty $X$ (the empty topology). No infinite-distance, semimetric or quasimetric convention is consumed.

items.title: Metric nonnegativity from the three axioms

references.title: Metric space (Wikipedia)
Ultrametric space (Wikipedia)
W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 2
T. Tao, Analysis II, 3rd ed., Ch. 1
Pseudometric space (Wikipedia)
R. Gardner, Introduction to Topology, notes on Munkres Section 20: The Metric Topology (East Tennessee State University)

items.statement: For any real metric or pseudometric $d$ on a set $X$ in [[def-emg-real-metric-axiom-convention]], $d(x,y)\ge0$ for every $x,y\in X$. Thus these three-axiom definitions already have values in $[0,\infty)$, including the vacuous assertion when $X=\varnothing$.

items.title: Explicit rational and real power regimes

references.title: J. Lebl, Basic Analysis I
Radicals and rational exponents (Emory University)
Exponentiation (Wikipedia)
Nth root (Wikipedia)
W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 1

items.statement:
For $a>0$, integer $m$ and integer $n\ge1$, define the rational regime by

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. The supplementary convention is $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$; $0^0$ and negative powers of zero remain undefined.

The separate real regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For $x>0$ set $0^x=0$; no arbitrary real power is assigned to a negative base. The real-power laws are supplied by that theorem, not inferred from the rational root formula. Use the real-number structure of [[def-real-numbers]].

In particular $s(q)=q^{1/2}$ for $q>0$ is the unique positive solution of $s(q)^2=q$. Its smoothness and derivative are a separate well-definedness result, not an assumption about fractional notation.

items.title: The positive square-root branch is smooth

references.title: J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, Theorem 8.5.1 and higher-regularity discussion

items.statement: For $q>0$, let $s(q)$ be the unique positive root specified in [[def-emg-explicit-power-regimes]]. Then $s:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is smooth and $s'(q)=1/(2s(q))$.

items.title: Sequence-limit criterion with explicit choice use

references.title: J. Lebl, Basic Analysis I, §3.1: Limits of functions
Limit of a function (Wikipedia)
W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 4 (Def. 4.1)
T. Tao, Analysis I, 3rd ed., §9.3
J. Lebl, Basic Analysis I, §3.1

items.statement: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, let $c\in\mathbb R$ be a limit point of $A$, let $f:A\to\mathbb R$ and $L\in\mathbb R$. Assume the indexed axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. Then the epsilon-delta condition $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L$ of [[def-function-limit]] is equivalent to the following: for every sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $x_n\in A\setminus\{c\}$ and $x_n\to c$, one has $f(x_n)\to L$. Sequence and sequence convergence mean [[def-sequence]] and [[def-real-limit]]. The forward direction uses no choice; the reverse direction uses only the stated indexed $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, not arbitrary-index choice.

items.title: Boundaryless domain for geometric completeness

references.title: Ved Datar, Lectures on Riemannian Geometry

items.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold **without boundary**, in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. Let $g$ be a positive definite smooth Riemannian metric as in [[def-riemannian-metric-symmetric-cotangent-connection-and-covariant-hessian]]. Use the Levi-Civita connection of [[def-levi-civita-connection]] with the existence and coordinate formula supplied by [[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]; in coordinates it has coefficients $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\frac12g^{kl}(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij})$. A parametrized affine geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:J\to M$ on an interval with nonempty interior satisfying $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$, equivalently $\ddot\gamma^k+\Gamma^k_{ij}(\gamma)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0$, where covariant differentiation along the curve is defined by [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]; the coordinate equation is the expansion of that derivative in a coordinate basis. Its maximal domain is an interval on which it cannot be extended with the same affine parameter as a solution. **Two-sided geodesic completeness** means that every maximal affine geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

Independently, for a real metric $d$ in [[def-metric-space]], a sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$ whenever $m,n\ge N$. It converges to $x$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ eventually $d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$. **Metric completeness** means that every Cauchy sequence converges in the given metric space. In a Riemannian application the metric must be the distance induced by $g$ on a connected component: the infimum of lengths $\int\sqrt{g(\dot\alpha,\dot\alpha)}\,dt$ over piecewise-$C^1$ connecting curves. Its definition and finite metric property are supplied by [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] and [[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]. Specify that induced metric, rather than an arbitrary compatible metric. Distinct components are treated separately; no infinite distance is inserted into a real metric.

These are different completeness conditions. Their equivalence is a Hopf–Rinow theorem requiring its own hypotheses and proof; it is not part of this definition. In particular, a Lorentzian metric is not a positive definite distance, and this convention supplies no Lorentzian Hopf–Rinow implication.

The boundaryless restriction matters: the Euclidean interval $[0,1]$ is metrically complete, while the curve $\gamma(t)=1/2+t$ stays inside it only for $-1/2\le t\le1/2$ and cannot be continued there as a two-sided affine geodesic with velocity $1$. Completeness of this interval follows because a real Cauchy sequence converges in $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] and its limit remains between $0$ and $1$. This boundary example explains the domain restriction; it is not an instance of the boundaryless equivalence.

items.title: Set-sized objects and definable-class schemas

references.title: B. Kaya, MATH 320 Set Theory (METU), §1.1
Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory (Wikipedia)
C. Wilson, A Brief Introduction to ZFC (Chicago REU 2016)

items.statement:
Use the first-order language of [[def-language-of-set-theory]]: all quantified objects are sets, and a **definable class** $\{x:\varphi(x,p)\}$ abbreviates a formula with set parameters $p$. It is not a new set or a domain for unrestricted quantification. Work with the usual set axioms, in particular [[def-axiom-of-power-set]] and [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], and the ordered pairs, products and functions of [[def-ordered-pair]], [[def-cartesian-product]] and [[def-function]]. The power-set axiom supplies a collecting set; Separation trims it to exactly $\mathcal P(X)=\{Y:Y\subseteq X\}$.

A **small category** has a set $O$ of objects, a set $A$ of arrows, source and target functions $s,t:A\to O$, an identity function $e:O\to A$, and a composition function on the set $\{(a,b)\in A\times A:s(a)=t(b)\}$, where $ab$ denotes $a\circ b$ and the laws are $s(e(x))=t(e(x))=x$, $s(ab)=s(b)$, $t(ab)=t(a)$, $e(t(a))a=a=ae(s(a))$, and $(ab)c=a(bc)$ whenever the displayed compositions are defined. It is **locally small** when each specified hom-collection is a set. A definable large category is a schema of formulas for its objects, arrows and operations, with those laws asserted as formulas; it is not a set of all objects or a category of all large categories. No Grothendieck universe is assumed.

All indexed families in the local bundle construction have a supplied set index $I$. If $U_i\subseteq M$ and $G$ is a set, their tagged disjoint union is the subset $D=\{(i,x,z)\in I\times M\times G:x\in U_i\}$, formed by Separation. Given a set equivalence relation $E\subseteq D\times D$, each class $[u]_E=\{v\in D:(u,v)\in E\}$ is a subset of $D$, and the quotient is the set

$$
D/E=\{C\in\mathcal P(D):\exists u\in D\ \forall v\in D\ (v\in C\iff(u,v)\in E)\}.
$$

Thus the quotient is obtained by Separation in $\mathcal P(D)$, without choosing representatives. Transition-map graphs and connection data are subsets of specified finite products and power sets, not arbitrary proper-class objects.

For the Cauchy-development coding application, fix a set manifold $\Sigma$ and the tensor-bundle total spaces over $\Sigma\times\mathbb R$. A code consists of an open set $D\subseteq\Sigma\times\mathbb R$, graphs of a metric and a two-form on $D$ inside those fixed total spaces, a time orientation, and a fixed initial embedding. All of its coordinates belong to fixed products and power sets. Separation selects the tuples satisfying the specified smoothness, Lorentzian, field-equation and initial-data formulas. Hence these codes form a set. This size assertion does not prove field-equation existence, maximality or uniqueness, and makes no proper-class representative choice.

items.title: Extended pointwise product with zero at infinite factors

references.title: Sheldon Axler, Measure, Integration & Real Analysis, extended-real multiplication convention

items.statement:
Let $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$ be the ordered set of [[def-extended-reals]]. Define a new total operation $\star:\overline{\mathbb R}\times\overline{\mathbb R}\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ as follows. If $a=0$ or $b=0$, put $a\star b=0$. If both factors are finite, put $a\star b=ab$ using real multiplication. In the remaining cases both factors are nonzero and at least one is infinite; put

$$a\star b:=\begin{cases}+\infty,&\operatorname{sgn}(a)\operatorname{sgn}(b)=1,\\-\infty,&\operatorname{sgn}(a)\operatorname{sgn}(b)=-1,\end{cases}$$

where $\operatorname{sgn}(a)=1$ for $a>0$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(a)=-1$ for $a<0$ in the extended order. The clauses exhaust the domain and agree when a zero factor is finite, so they specify a unique value for every pair. Thus $0\star(\pm\infty)=0$, $(+\infty)\star(-2)=-\infty$, and $(-\infty)\star(-\infty)=+\infty$.

For any set $X$ and maps $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$, their **extended pointwise product with zero at infinite factors** is the map $f\star g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ defined by $(f\star g)(x)=f(x)\star g(x)$.

items.title: Lp classes and explicit representatives

references.title: Sheldon Axler, Measure, Integration & Real Analysis, Definition 7.17 and Theorem 7.18

items.statement:
Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space in [[def-measure-space]]. A measurable real function is a map $f:X\to\mathbb R$ measurable from $(X,\Sigma)$ to the real Borel measurable space, in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. For $1\le p<\infty$, use the measurable real functions satisfying $\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty$; for $p=\infty$, use the essentially bounded measurable real functions, meaning that $\mu(\{x:|f(x)|>C\})=0$ for some finite $C\ge0$.

On either function space put

$$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu(\{x\in X:f(x)\ne g(x)\})=0.$$

The inequality set is measurable for real measurable functions. The relation and quotient are precisely those of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. The element $[f]\in L^p(\mu)$ is the equivalence class of $f$; an **explicit representative** is a specified measurable function belonging to that class. The quotient norms are

$$\|[f]\|_p=\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad\|[f]\|_\infty=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_X|f|,$$

with independence of representative and the norm axioms supplied by [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]].

A pointwise statement such as $f(x)=0$ concerns the selected representative. A property invariant under almost-everywhere equality, such as $f=0$ almost everywhere, concerns the class. No value of $[f]$ at a particular point is defined by this quotient.

items.title: Local potentials and smooth circle-bundle connection data
items.statement:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

By [[def-de-rham-cohomology]], $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^2(M)/B^2(M)$, where $Z^2(M)$ is the vector space of closed smooth two-forms and $B^2(M)$ is the vector space of exact smooth two-forms. Thus, for closed $F$, the statement $[F]=0$ means exactly that $F=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$. This equivalence is the quotient definition; it does not assert that every closed form is exact.

Let $U(1)=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ with complex multiplication, the subspace topology and the usual smooth circle structure. A **normalized circle-connection datum** on $M$ consists of a supplied countable open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, smooth transition maps $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U(1)$, smooth real one-forms $a_i\in\Omega^1(U_i)$, and a fixed constant $\kappa_0>0$. Require $g_{ii}=1$ and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on every triple intersection. Around each point of $U_i\cap U_j$, a smooth real phase lift $f_{ij}$ exists with $g_{ij}=e^{if_{ij}}$; require

$$
a_j=a_i+df_{ij}
$$

on every such phase-lift neighborhood. Different lifts differ locally by an integer multiple of $2\pi$, so their differentials agree and this compatibility condition is independent of the lift. Equivalently, with the globally defined real one-form $\lambda(g)=-i\,g^{-1}dg$ on each overlap, the condition is $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$.

The circle is a smooth Lie group and in particular a topological group: multiplication is the restriction of continuous complex multiplication and inversion is complex conjugation. A right principal $U(1)$-bundle has a continuous right action and locally trivial equivariant product charts; those charts make the action free and transitive on each fibre, as defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]. The compatible transition functions are the gluing data for such a bundle, in the convention that a point with fibre coordinate $z_i$ in chart $i$ has coordinate $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$ in chart $j$. No global real-valued angle on $U(1)$ is assumed.

The constant $\kappa_0$ is a chosen normalization with units of webers; it is not Planck's constant and is not a unit of electric charge. On a chart whose coordinates have length units, the normalized connection components $a_i$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding local potential $A_i:=\kappa_0a_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and its curvature $F_i:=dA_i=\kappa_0\,da_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. This definition imposes no flux or charge quantization.

items.title: Radial primitives for closed one- and two-forms
items.statement:
Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be an open set star-shaped about $p\in D$, meaning $p+t(x-p)\in D$ for every $x\in D$ and $0\le t\le1$. Let $F=\frac12F_{ab}\,dx^a\wedge dx^b$ be a smooth real closed two-form on $D$. Use Einstein summation over coordinate indices $a,b,c\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Define

$$
A_b(x):=\int_0^1 t(x-p)^aF_{ab}(p+t(x-p))\,dt.
$$

Then $A=A_b\,dx^b$ is a smooth real one-form on $D$ and $dA=F$. More generally, if $\alpha=\alpha_a dx^a$ is a smooth closed one-form on $D$, then

$$
\chi(x):=\int_0^1(x-p)^a\alpha_a(p+t(x-p))\,dt
$$

is smooth and $d\chi=\alpha$. The first formula gives a local potential for every smooth closed two-form in a star-shaped coordinate chart; it does not assert global exactness.

references.title: Victor Guillemin and Peter Haine, Differential Forms, MIT 18.952 text (2019), sections 2.4 and 2.6
references.locator: Section 2.4, coordinate exterior derivative and d²=0, printed pp. 53–57; section 2.6, homotopy operator and Poincaré consequence, printed pp. 61–65.

items.title: Circle gluing, curvature and connection variations
items.statement: Let $M$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable oriented four-manifold, and let $(U_i,g_{ij},a_i;\kappa_0)$ be a normalized circle-connection datum as in [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]]. Use the set-sized-object and quotient convention of [[def-emg-set-size-and-class-schema]]. Then the chart data construct a smooth Hausdorff second-countable right principal $U(1)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and a global smooth real connection one-form $\omega$ on $P$. Its curvature is basic: there is a smooth closed two-form $f\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $d\omega=\pi^*f$ and $f|_{U_i}=da_i$. The local potentials $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ satisfy $dA_i=F$, where $F=\kappa_0 f$ is global. For two connections on the same fixed bundle with the same transition functions, their local-form differences are restrictions of one global base one-form; adding a global one-form to all local representatives stays in that bundle sector.

items.title: Sphere winding, nonexact curvature and flat holonomy
items.statement:
For $b\in\mathbb R$, let $M=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, $r=(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, and define the smooth real two-form

$$
F_b:=\frac{b}{r^3}\left(x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy\right).
$$

Use the standard product smooth structure and orientation on $M$; it is an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, hence smooth, Hausdorff and second-countable.

Let $U_N=\{(x^0,x,y,z)\in M:r+z>0\}$ and $U_S=\{(x^0,x,y,z)\in M:r-z>0\}$; these two open sets cover $M$. Then $dF_b=0$ and its flux through the unit sphere with outward orientation is $4\pi b$. If $b\ne0$, $F_b$ has no global one-form potential on $M$. On $U_N$ and $U_S$,

$$
A_N=b(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad A_S=-b(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi
$$

are smooth local potentials with $dA_N=dA_S=F_b$, and $A_S-A_N=-2b\,d\phi$ on the overlap. For a chosen normalization $\kappa_0>0$, these local forms define the normalized circle-connection data of [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]] precisely when the transition $g_{NS}=e^{-2ib\phi/\kappa_0}$ is single-valued, equivalently $2b/\kappa_0\in\mathbb Z$. For a smooth loop $g(e^{i\phi})=e^{i\chi(\phi)}$, its winding is $[\chi(2\pi)-\chi(0)]/(2\pi)$, with both circles oriented by increasing angle. Existence of a smooth phase lift, integrality of its endpoint change, and independence of the lift are proved in the phase-lift construction below. The transition winding has sign $-2b/\kappa_0$ in the stated north-to-south convention, while $\int_{S^2}F_b/(2\pi\kappa_0)=2b/\kappa_0$. This is an exact condition for this chosen circle normalization, not a claim that every classical real flux is quantized. When $2b/\kappa_0\in\mathbb Z$, the compatible two-set data also produce a smooth principal circle-bundle connection, using the actual set-size interface in [A1] and the gluing statement of [[lem-emg-circle-connection-gluing]].

There is also a flat example with nontrivial holonomy. On $M_0=\mathbb R\times S^1\times\mathbb R^2$, let $\nu=-i w^{-1}dw$ be the global angular one-form on the base circle $S^1=\{w\in\mathbb C:|w|=1\}$, normalized by $\int_{S^1}\nu=2\pi$, and take $A=\kappa_0 a\,\nu$ for dimensionless $a\in\mathbb R$. On the trivial bundle use $\omega=\vartheta+a\pi^*\nu$, where $\vartheta=-i z^{-1}dz$ is the fibre angular form. Holonomy means the fibre multiplier of the horizontal lift around the indicated base loop; gauge trivial means gauge-equivalent to $\vartheta$ under a smooth bundle map $G_u(x,z)=(x,z u(x))$ covering the identity. Then $F=dA=0$ but holonomy around the circle is $e^{-2\pi ia}$, so this connection is gauge trivial exactly when $a\in\mathbb Z$. If $b$ and $\kappa_0$ are assigned physical units, both are measured in webers; the ratio $2b/\kappa_0$ is dimensionless. No general classification of circle bundles is asserted.

items.title: Nonexact sphere flux and circle winding
items.statement:
Use the conditional, still-escalated draft result [[lem-emg-sphere-flux-holonomy]] with $b=\kappa_0/2$. Its authored supplier status and remaining external closure obligation are recorded below; no independent proof acceptance is asserted. The local potentials are

$$
A_N=\frac{\kappa_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad A_S=-\frac{\kappa_0}{2}(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.
$$

They have common curvature $F=\frac{\kappa_0}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$, flux $2\pi\kappa_0$, and transition $g_{NS}=e^{-i\phi}$ of winding number $-1$ under the north-to-south convention. The example is a mathematical circle-connection patch model. It is not an observation of a magnetic monopole and makes no quantum or empirical claim.
